div.head: W e present the Response-Time Analysis ( R T A ) method for providing real-time guarantees in Asynchronous Transfer Mode ( A T M ) communication networks, and evaluates its suitability for use in hard real-time factory-type environments. R T A provides an analysis of the network trafic which can be used by an admission control mechanism to determine if the timing requirements of a new connection can be guaranteed without violating the requirements of already admitted connections. This type of admission control is required by several multimedia and almost all real-time control applications. R T A is based on traditional fixed-priority/rate-monotonic real-time CPU schedulability analysis. This makes it possible to combine communication analysis with CPU schedulability analysis, thus
div.p: allowing system designers to use the same technique for assessing the timely behaviour of the entire system, including both CPU and network scheduling. The only assumption R T A makes about the ATM-network is that the switches should be equipped with prioritised output queues, something which is true for many commercial switches.

The main focus of this paper is on evaluating RTA. I n the evaluation we compare R T A with Weighted Fair Queueing ( W F Q ) and the Calculus of Network Delays (CND). W F Q is the currently most popular method for providing performance guarantees, and C N D provides an alternative analysis for prioritised queueing. The comparison shows that RTA outperforms both W F Q and C N D for a set of realistic trafic scenarios.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The use of communication networks in modern factories is rapidly increasing. Many applications using the services of these networks have strict timing requirements. This include applications related to the command and control of equipment used in the production process. For these applications, statistical guarantees, e.g. in terms of "message loss probabil.ity" or "average message delay", are not sufficient. Instead, a firmer commitment is needed from the network, saying that it will always deliver all messages completely and within specified deadlines (with reservation for hardware failure and external physical interference). Several methods for providing such guarantees have been proposed in the literature [Go190, DKS90, PG93, PG94, ZF94, RMZ94, RMZ95, Kar96, SL96, SMT96, HST971. They all provide or assume some mechanism of bandwidth sha.ring and have an associated analysis that can be used by an admission control procedure to d priori answer the crucial question: 0-71303-4 182-1/97/$10.00 01997 IEEE Can the QoS requirements of a new connection be met, while not violating the requirements of already admitted connections?

A positive answer means that the connection can be admitted. A negative answer means that if the new connection is admitted the QoS of the new connection, as well as the &OS of already admitted connections, may be violated. It is important that solutions to the real-time admission control problem can be easily incorporated with existing network standards. It must also be possible to make efficient implementations, supporting the very high bandwidth of current and future networks. Furthermore, an admission control scheme must allow for high utilisation of network resources. Since not all connections may require absolute guarantees it should be possible to integrate hard real-time traffic with other &OS classes which do not require absolute guarantees on the timely delivery of messages. An additional benefit would be if the analysis could be incorporated with an existing framework for real-time systems analysis. This would allow system designers t o use the same technique for assessing the timely behaviour of the entire system, including both CPU and network scheduling.

In this paper we propose an extended version of the Response-Time Analysis (RTA) method introduced in [HST97]. RTA has been developed for admission control of hard real-time traffic in ATM networks. In [HST97] we present RTA for single-switch ATM networks with unique priorities for each connection. In this paper we outline a generalisation of RTA to handle multiple switch ATM networks and also to allow several streams to share priority.

We have focused on ATM, since it is likely that ATM will be used in industrial control systems and other safety critical applications, simply because it will be the cheapest high bandwidth communication technology available. Also, ATM is an attractive solution in industrial environments due to its optical transmission media, avoiding electrical signalling which in these harsh environments may be error prone.

The main focus of this paper is on evaluating RTA, rather than providing a very detailed presentation. Since the QoS-guarantee methods are different in character, each have their strong and weak points, analytically proving that one method is better than another is not a viable evaluation method. Instead we use a "benchmarking"-type of evaluation, in which a limited number of realistic scenarios are used to compare the different methods.

RTA is attractive since it uses a very simple priority queueing mechanism that provides a clear separation between bandwidth and deadline requirements. This gives RTA a potential of offering a bandwidth utilisation outperforming currently popular bandwidth reservation schemes, such as Weighted Fair Queueing (WFQ) [DKSSO, PG93, PG941. We test this hypothesis by comparing RTA and WFQ for some realistic traffic scenarios. In addition, we compare RTA with the Calculus of Network De-Iays (CND) [CruSlI, which is an alternative analysis method when using priority queueing.

Paper Outline: In Section 2 we give a brief introduction to ATM and the considered methods for providing hard real-time guarantees in ATM networks. Section 3 presents the traffic model we use in our evaluation. In Section 4, we outline the extended Response-Time Analysis (RTA) method, and in Section 5 we describe the scenarios we have used in our evaluation of the different call admission methods. Section 6 presents the results of the evaluation, and finally, in Section 7 we discuss our results, draw some conclusions, and indicate possible future work.

div.head: ATM and Real-Time
div.p: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) [HHS94] is a high performance, connection oriented, network architecture. Over each connection a stream of fixed size packets, called cells, are transmitted. Each cell is 53 bytes long, consisting of 5 byte header information -t 48 byte payload (user data). Long messages are segmented and sent in consecutive cells in the stream. The ATM network guarantees that cells within a stream is delivered in the same order as they were transmitted.

An ATM network consists of a set of ATM switches. Each switch routes cells from a set of input ports to a set of output ports based on stream identifiers in the cell-headers. At the output port of an ATM switch a port controller multiplexes cells from different streams onto the outgoing line.

The output ports of an ATM switch are governed by a scheduling policy, e.g. First In, First Out (FIFO), which decides what cells to dequeue from the output queue. Scheduling policies can be classified as either work-conserving or non work-conserving. A work-conserving policy never let the output link go idle if there are cells queued in the output queue, whereas a non work-conserving policy may let the link go idle even if the output queue is non-empty. An example of a work-conserving policy is FIFO, and an example of a non work-conserving policy is Golestanis " .

All work-conserving policies have identical average cell delay, average and maximum buffer need (for any given set of cell arrival pattern). A non work-conserving policy must by necessity have higher average cell delay, average and maximum buffer need than a work-conserving policy. On the other hand, work-conserving policies tends to increases the burstiness of the traffic, while non work-conserving policies can be used to limit burstiness.

ATM has been designed to support the high bandwidth, optical signalling, of todays and future information super highways. The stream/cell concept have been designed to allow efficient hardware implementations. ATM is proposed as the next generation global telecom network. This network should support a number of communications services, including phone calls, video conferencing and computer communication. ATM is also used for a Local Area Networks (LANs) [Par94, Sec. 6.31.

Clearly, fulfilling all these requirements is not an easy task. Different applications have different timing and bandwidth requirements. To make sure that each application gets the required Quality of Service (QoS) the network must perform some form of admission control on new streams. The admission control should ensure that there are enough resources in the network t o give the new stream its required QoS, without compromising the QoS of other (already ad-mit ted) streams.

To provide a guaranteed &OS, the ATM network needs to test whether or not the requested &OS of each stream can be guaranteed. This test is cadled "Call Admission Control" (CAC). There exists many methods for performing the CAC, however, most methods only give statistical guarantees, e.g. in terms of "average cell delay". For hard real-time traffic where the &OS must be an absolute guarantees these type of CACs are not applicable. Instead, a deterministic guarantee, e.g. guaranteeing that ''the deadline is never missed", is needed. In this paper we only consider methods to provide deterministic &OS guarantees.

To perform the CAC an analysis method is required. Each analysis method is intimately related t o a scheduling policy. For some scheduling policies there many different types of analysis methods, while other scheduling policies have a single analysis method which has been developed together with the scheduling policy.

Our focus in this paper is on work-conserving scheduling policies. Since, as a general rule, workconserving policies are easier to implement and re- quires simpler buffer management. Thus, making them more suitable for ATM networks. Workconserving scheduling policies can roughly be classified as either: Common for all rate based scheduling policies is that the response-time is directly dependent on the service rate allocated to the stream, and the service rate corresponds directly to the bandwidth allocation. Thus, to lower the response-time one must allocate more bandwidth. For streams with tight deadline this may lead to over-allocation of bandwidth, since the stream need t o allocate more bandwidth than it is going to use, in order to lower the response-time.

Most rate-based scheduling policies have quite simple analysis methods. However, implementations of these scheduling policies are often very complex. Today, rate-based scheduling is not a viable solution in ATM networks. However, recent hardware research [SVCSS] indicate that it will be possible to produce cost effective rate-based ATM switches in the future. Today, the rate-based WFQ is being implemented in Internet routers.

In this paper we present an evaluation the Response-Time Ana1,ysis (RTA) presented in Section 4. For comparison we also evaluate two other analysis methods. Those methods are: the analysis presented in [PG93, PG94] for Weighted Fair Queueing (WFQ), and Cruz's Calculus for Network Delays [CruSl] for FIFO and priority queueing (PRIQ).

We have chosen WFQ to represent the rate-base service disciplines since it is the most well known of the methods. Also, it is the method which closes approximat,e Generalised Processor Sharing (GPS). CND has been evaluated since it is an alternative method to RTA.

Since both CND and RTA both are applicable to both FIFO and PRIQ we will study both methods on both scheduling policies. We use the notational convention to append the name of the scheduling policy to the name of the analysis method, e.g. RTA-PRIQ.

For RT.A-PRIQ and CND-PRIQ the algorithm presented in [Sj097] is used to assign priorities. The algorithm i,s a heuristic and do not guarantee an optimal priority assignment. (No optimal priority as- signment scheme exist for distributed systems.)

div.head: Measuring Performance
div.p: Since we are studying the problem of B priori determine if deadlines will be met we are not really interested in the scheduling policy, instead we focus on the analysis methods. As mentioned in Section 1 doing a general analytical comparison of the different methods is not possible, SO we resort to "benchmarking", using simulations to generate traffic scenarios.

A good way to understand how well an analysis method performs is to study how much of the network resources it allows to be allocated before the Call Admission Control (CAC) fails. In our comparison the CAC is performed for scenarios consisting of whole set of streams. The CAC is successful if all streams in the scenario can be guaranteed to meet their respective deadlines.

We will study the admission probability (introduced by Raha,Malcom and Zhao [RMZ94]) curve for each method. The admission probability for a specific level of network load is defined as the probability of performing a successful CAC for a scenario with that load.

Naturally, the admission probability is highly dependent on the profile of the streams in the scenario. If the scenarios contains many streams with tight deadlines, the admission probability can be very low even for low network loads. Ideally, the admission probability should be 1.0 for any network load, including a load of loo%, but for most realistic scenarios this will not be the case for any analysis method. In our study we use 4 different traffic profiles, these are described in Section 5.3.
In this study we only consider the delay in the cell spacer and the network output queues.

div.head: Results of Benchmarking
div.p: In this section we present the admission probability curves for the above four scenarios. Figure 2 From the figures it is evident that RTA outperforms all the other analysis methods and that PRIQ has vastly better performance than FIFO.

The fact that CND performs worse than RTA (both for PRIQ and FIFO) is not very surprising since CND uses a traffic model which is more pessimistic than RTA's traffic model. A bit more surprising is the amount by which RTA-PRIQ outperforms CND-PRIQ (CND-PRIQ performs similarly t o WFQ in all the investigated profiles). Since both analysis methods assume PRIQ the large performance difference is solely due t o the difference in precession in the traffic models.

Even more surprising is the poor performance of WFQ. This is surprising since WFQ often is ad- vocated, in the computer-and tele-communication communities, as the solution to provide QoS guarantees. However, to achieve high utilisation of the network resources (at least in real-time scenarios) RTA-PRIQ must be preferred before WFQ.

Another interesting fact, is that RTA-PRIQ have a very high admission probability up until some (profile dependent) network load. For instance, in "Control 2" (in Figure 3) the admission probability is almost l, if the network load is below 80%. For all the other methods, the admission probability is a steadily decreasing function as the network load increases. For a real-time system developer this aspect of RTA-PRIQ is very important, since when starting to design a system, information needed to perform the actual CAC is not available. However, it might be possible to guess the network load at an early stage, thus allowing the developer asses that the network load stays below the threshold when admission probability starts to decrease.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We have presented and evaluated an extension of the RTA method for admission control analysis in ATM networks. RTA uses traditional real-time response-time type analysis [JP86, ABD+95] to cal-culate the worst-case response time of ATM-cells sent through an ATM-network using priority queued output buffers in the switches.

The introduced RTA-extensions allow analysis of muhti-switch networks with a limited number of priority levels. The latter implies that several connections may have to share priority, i.e., priority as- signments ranging from a single priority (pure FIFO scheduling) to a unique priority per connection can be handled. This means that many realistic network and traffic situations can be analysed.

IRTA provides a solutions to the real-time admission control problem which be easily incorporated with existing network standards, in fact several existing ATM-switches already today provide the required priority queueing. An additional benefit is that the analysis can be incorporated with existing frameworks (e.g. Fixed Priority Scheduling [AB;D+95]) for real-time system schedulability analysis, thereby allowing system designers to use the same technique for assessing the timely behaviour of the entire system, including both CPU and network scheduling.

In the evaluation we compared RTA with two other methods for hard real-time admission control. The first of these, Weighted Fair Queueing (WFQ), makes fixed bandwidth allocations to guarantee both bandwidth and delay requirements. This is in contrast with RTA and the second compared method, the Calculus of Network Delays (CND), which both uses priorities to control the traffic flow. Priorities allow separate treatment of bandwidth and delay requirements. An additional benefit with priority queueing is its efficient integration of hard real-time trafic with other QoS classes which do not require absolute guarantees. Non hard real-time traffic is simply assigned lower priority, meaning bothi that it will not interfere with the hard real-time traffic and thak it can use any bandwidth not used by the realtime traffic. Efficient bandwidth sharing between critical and non-critical traffic is less obvious for rate bxjed reservation schemes, such as WFQ.

In the evaluation we used a traffic scenario profile resembling traffic in a real-time system. Sets of traffic scenarios conforming to the profile characteristics were generated. We then performed the Controll Admission Control (CAC) for all three methodis on the generated traffic scenarios to calculate admission probabilities for different network loads, i.e , the probability of performing a successful CAC for a scenario with that load. The resulting comparisons show that RTA has higher admission probabilities than both WFQ and CND. In fact, since we have compared RTA with the best methods known t o us, the comparison gives evidence that RTA allows higher utilisation of network resources than any otlher known method. Thus, it seems that RTA from this perspective is the best existing method.

On the other hand, we also made the observation that WFQ provides the fastest CAC. Performing an RTA CAC can sometimes be more than 100 times slower than a WFQ CAC. The reason for this difference is that the RTA CAC for each connection have to consider the interference from all other connections in the network, while the WFQ CAC for a connection can be made independently of other connections.

In conclusion, RTA allows higher utilisation of network resources than other methods, but the CAC execution time must be improved if RTA is to be used in larger networks with dynamically arriving connections.

On the hand, the majority of hard real-time systems (e.g. :systems for process control) are quite small and typically have a relatively static set of hard realtime connections. For these type of systems, RTA seems already today the best alternative for providing hard real-time guarantees.

note.p: Most "simple" scheduling policies are not simple at all t o analyse. It is often very hard, sometimes impossible, to determine the end-toend response-times for messages when simple policies are used. Example of analysis methods for FIFO and priority queueing are Cruz's Calculus for Network Delays (CND)[Crugl] and our Response-Time Analysis (RTA). For EDF the methods presented in [FV90] can be applied to ATM networks. 0 Rate Based Scheduling Policies In rate based policies each stream is allocated a service rate or a weight. The rate (or weight) determines how much resources are allocated to the stream. As a rule, rate based scheduling policies approximate the idealised service discipline Generalised Processor Sharing (GPS). Some example of the class of GPS approximative scheduling policies are: Virtual Clock (VC) [Zha90], Weighted Fair Queueing (WFQ) [DKSSO], Weighted Round Robin (WRR) [RMZ95], Slow Start GPS [SL96] and Multirate PGPS [SMT96].
